newsitem.title: CHINA: China stares down heavenly dog in solar eclipse.
newsitem.headline: China stares down heavenly dog in solar eclipse.

text.p: Residents of China's capital Beijing took to the streets on Sunday to view a rare solar eclipse, an event that legend holds is caused by a hungry dog feasting on the sun.
Sun-gazers in Beijing saw a partial eclipse that gobbled up about half of the early morning sun.

Scientists and amateur astronomers who made the trek to Mohe, about 1,500 km (950 miles) to the northeast in the chilly province of Heilongjiang, were treated to a total eclipse that began at 9.07 a.m. (0107 GMT) and lasted more than two minutes.
"The Chinese say an eclipse is caused by a heavenly dog that eats the sun," said a Beijing office worker.
"People used to beat drums and shout to scare the dog away and make the sun come back," he said.
Authorities had set up three observation sites in Mohe and organised special trains to carry curious sky-watchers from the provincial capital of Harbin, the Xinhua news agency said.
State television carried live broadcasts of the eclipse from Mohe and major cities throughout China and official media warned people not to look directly at the sun without eye protection.
Beijing residents gathered in parks or on sidewalks to view the eclipse, many staring at the heavenly sight through film negatives or sunglasses.
Solar eclipses have traditionally augured bad news in China, where spectacular natural events such as earthquakes, floods and comets are thought to herald big political change.
The death of Chairman Mao Zedong in September 1976 was preceded in July by a huge earthquake in Tangshan that killed at least 270,000 people.
Mao's successor Deng Xiaoping died last month aged 92.
"But the eclipse has occurred after Deng's death, so there's no way to prove a connection," the office worker said.
